hook: Deleting apps is not a phone detox. It is just a harder login.
topic: Why app deletion fails as a strategy
body:
**Deleting apps is not a phone detox. It is just a harder login.**

When you delete Instagram, the app is gone. But the trained neural pathway that reaches for it is not. The dopamine loop is still running. The reflex still fires every time you hit a moment of low stimulation or mild discomfort. All you have done is put one extra step between the reflex and the reward.

For three days, the extra step works. Then you reinstall. And the reinstall takes 45 seconds.

This is because the problem was never the app. The app is a delivery mechanism. The problem is the environment that makes reaching for the delivery mechanism the path of least resistance.

The counterintuitive move is not to remove access. It is to increase the cost of access systematically. Delete the app — but also log out of the browser version. Use a separate email for the account. Add a screen time passcode that someone else sets. Each additional step degrades the automaticity of the reflex because the reflex is looking for low-friction execution.

You are not removing the destination. You are making the route expensive enough that the reflex dies before it gets there.

That distinction is what separates a protocol that holds from one that lasts a weekend.
